Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is an introduction to the essay for the five assumptions made by behaviourist approaches in counselling and show how these aid counselors to achieve counselling objectives?
Answer: Wow. Used to see a lot more junior high request for fake homework assignments. And you’re British (the spellings.) I’m disappointed.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it normal to have a crush on your counselor/therapist? How should one handle this situation?
Answer: Happens a lot. Why wouldn’t it? Therapy can be a wonderful, caring, safe and comforting place. What to do, especially if it’s become a distraction. Same thing we do with a variety of issues. Express: Bring it up. Explore: Discuss it. Openly, gently, clearly. In the exploration, you take a step back and lookat things clearly and objectively. Resolve. The typical resolution starts in the exploration — Doing that, maybe a few times, cools the flames of desire and fantasy, and leads to learning something useful, both to the therapy and relationships in general.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it necessary for therapists to keep their phones on during therapy sessions?
Answer: No, absolutely not. Talk about serious emergencies? Let’s say I’m solo. No staff. The insurance agency down the hall has a good size staff. I sweet-talked my friend Jack there, who always answers his phone during work hours. My 2 key people have HIS number, and in a genuinely dire emergency that demands my presence they’ll call Jack, and Jack will come over and knock on my door. In three years Jack never had to do that. A friend has a dedicated cellphone, and only two people have the number. It’s set to flash. Her wife and adult son can call her on that phone, and never, ever do. Except that one time. I’m so old I worked with no phone in my pocket at all. I was on call at a hospital, and was excited when I got a beeper. Nothing horrible happened. No, therapists do not need to be tethered to their phone during sessions. Those who do make it clear to the client that even those expensive, soul searching 50 minutes aren’t as important as that phone on the desk, and the therapist isn’t smart enough to figure out an alternative.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What happens if you don't feel like therapy is working for you? Do you have to continue with the sessions?
Answer: Of course not, but don’t quit until you’ve done an assessment. Tell the therapist you feel things aren’t working, and you want to explore that together by taking a look that the process so far, and how it could be improved. You’re both likely to have some ideas, and together you may be able to create something really useful for you.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Why do I keep forgetting the question my therapist asks after starting to answer it?
Answer: Well, I’m the guy who teaches therapists not to ask question, which are a controlling way of taking charge of the therapy and deciding what you should talk about. That’s really your decision, not theirs. If you absolutely feel the need to control the client in that way, you can at least soften it: “I have to admit I’ve really curious about what your dad was like.” That’s information about me, not a command for you to obey. It’s up to you. Forgetting the question? Just guessing, but that would be a good example of healthy resistance. Resistance (conscious or not) is a way a client can managed the speed, depth of interpretation or choice of topics, enough to make the session suit better, feel safer, and empower the client.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: I’ve been 4 months in therapy for trauma and I can’t seem to open up. I’m like a terrified child and I’m so embarrassed. I can’t even sit in the chair without panicking for half the session. Is this normal? I feel like I’m totally failing
Answer: So, so very sorry to hear about this. My first instinct is to guess that it’s the therapist who’s doing the “failing.” Situational anxiety tends to be fairly easy to treat and reduce, and most therapists know how to do it. There a literally dozens of effective techniques. Four months — that’s what’s upsetting me. No, it’s not normal, and no, you’re not failing. And by the way you don’t have to “open up” — a lot of helpful therapy can happen with the client “opening up.” Besides, all those anxiety symptoms are in a sense a way of opening up. An early way, yes, but you’ve created an opening that any therapist, especially any half-way decent trauma therapist, should be able to handle in ways that help you get to where you’d like to go.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Should I be mad my therapist had someone else message me (from front desk) to switch my appointment time instead of him doing it himself? He’s emailed me before, so why not now? It infuriates me for some reason.
Answer: I’m like a lot of psychologists/therapists. I never made or changed my appointments, at any place I ever worked, nor did anybody I worked with. Our support staff is available more or less all day to take and make calls, along with other jobs, whereas we therapists are in with clients. Don’t you want your therapist to be undistracted and focused only on you during your session times? Don’t you want to be able to call in to staff and check or change your appointment? Some therapists do all the clerical work themselves, including scheduling, but most of us prefer to be able to focus full time on our clients, like doctors and dentists etc.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: My friends call me retarded and an idiot and always bring me down. What should I do?
Answer: They are not your friends. A friend is someone who likes you and cares about you, and wants the best for you. A friend spends happy times with you and sometimes shares sad times too, and gives support, and watches out for you. People who subject you to emotional abuse are the opposite of friends. There are friends out there waiting to meet you, even though it may take a little time for you to find them. What you should do is join a club or an organization or church group, or volunteer association, or work at a food shelf — any place you’ll find people who are interested in things you are interested in. That’s were many people meet friends.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How can therapists effectively work with shame in a way that leads to healing rather than further shame spirals?
Answer: Treat for the basic anxiety first, if the symptoms are available, and maintain a solid, close working relationship with the client. Some shame-based folks respond well to a cognitive approach (in a strong therapy relationship). Shame of course flows from thinking thoughts that just continue the endless cycle. “I caused the company to go under, and 200 people lost their jobs! I’ll never get over the guilt (translate “shame.) Basic cognitive reframing, it the therapy relationship is good, can often help.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it acceptable to terminate a therapist-patient relationship for personal reasons rather than professional ones?
Answer: Three would be very few “professional reasons” to dump a client, and unless you do it very carefully, you could get in trouble and be accused of unethical abandonment. Dangerous, disruptive, scary stalker clients, yes, but those are pretty rare. It’s usually personal reasons. I’m going for a big spinal surgery and I won’t be able to go back to work, even online work, for several months. I’m moving to Canada. I’m going back for a full time Ph.D. program, in pursuit of a psychologist license and an academic career. All kinds of obvious things.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists have favorite clients? How does this affect their work and how can clients recognize and address this preference in therapy?
Answer: I can have 3 different favorite clients before lunch. It’s not that hard to get into a client and their session, and have a great experience, though I have to confess the clients that just about always become (temporary) super favorites — kids ages 4–7 “Favorite” status is very short term thing. It has to be. If I’m going to be a consistently effective, I can’t be dwelling on someone I saw last Thursday. In this business you develop some healthy habits, like the person with you at the time is your current favorite. That habit is one of the things that makes therapy a joy.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it possible for clients to fire their therapists without a valid reason, simply because they want to switch to a different therapist?
Answer: It is absolutely possible. The client is the boss, and they don’t have to give a “valid reason” for firing us. And if they want to switch to a new therapist, that’s “valid” enough fo me. I’m not saying it’s a good idea, and nobody’s asking me — but it’s certainly possible, even if it’s not polite, or even if the client is missing a critical final session with the previous guy — those final summary sessions can be very useful, at lest sometimes.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can a therapist end a session or terminate the therapeutic relationship based on something said during an appointment?
Answer: Yes. I had a non-client called Cal who brought an enormous loaded handgun into his what would have been his first session (Sig Sauer P-228 — why is that imprinted on my brain?). In spite of the fact that the clinic was posted, which made bringing the gun inside llegal, he was determined to lecture me on the Second Amendment and his liberties, etc., as he showed me his. . .weapon. He said there was no way in hell he was going to leave his gun in his car, much less at home. I reminded him we had not entered into any kind of psychotherapy relationship, and in fact had never had one, or any agreement so far, and our only topic had been gun laws. I said that I wouldn’t be allowed by the owners to become his therapist or permit him on the premises if it was his intention to bring a gun into the clinic. (I didn’t mention that I was an owner). He persisted. I excused myself for an urgent potty break, during which I called 911 and had a 20 second conversation (we were a few blocks from the local precinct). I returned to my office and announced I had made a complaint that a man with a gun was in our posted clinic, but not actively threatening anyone, and seemed calm. I requested discreet but immediate police assistance. Two officers showed up in about 90 seconds, had a low-key conversation with the non-client, and escorted him out. One of them returned in about 20 minutes to tell us they had warned the guy to stay at least 1000 feet away from our clinic, armed or not, and that they would be watching for him. Fortunately, that’s the end of the story. They don’t teach anything about this kind of thing in therapy school. It wasn’t until the next day that it occurred to me to wonder why Sig Sauer Guy wanted therapy (if he actually did), and of course I’ll never know.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it considered ethical for a therapist to diagnose someone without meeting them in person?
Answer: I’m trying to think of situations where it could be ethical. Let’s say a supervisee is introducing case (no names or identifying details) and she’s tending to think in terms of a Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) diagnosis, and wants my opinion about someone I will never see or know. Maybe I’ll say “have you thought of cyclothymia, or Bipolar 2, or maybe an atypical anxiety disorder, or. . .?” I’m just tossing out ideas about a real human I’m never going to meet. That would be ethical. Here’s where it could be unethical. A client is complaining about his wife. He’s listing, in simple language, what sound to me a lot like the criteria for BPD. You have to meet five of the nine to get the diagnosis. I’m hearing at least seven or eight. There is no way I’m going to say the words “Borderline Personality Disorder,” but I’m definitely going to support my client in managing an emotionally difficult situation, and if he starts talking about BPD, we’ll chat, but there’s no way I’m going to put a label on someone I’ve never seen.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it common for therapists to refuse to provide letters of absence for their clients?
Answer: Not in the US. I figure you might be from the UK or Australia (I’ve never heard of “letters of absence.”) Therapists, even psychologists, tend to avoid writing “medical excuses.” We’re not medical, and not formally qualified to evaluate health conditions and whether or not a client could or should perform certain duties. There are also complex legal, ethical, and related reasons that make us reluctant to disclose specific reasons. You doctor can say you broke your leg and would be able to run your fork lift for three weeks. If a therapist is required to provide a reason for an absence or an inability to do some task, it will require disclosing protected health information of a much different sort than a broken femur. Your employer doesn’t need to know the details of your anxiety disorder, or your progress with drugs for your manic episodes, etc.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it okay to meet with a few different therapists before deciding who to continue with?
Answer: It’s highly recommended. There’s a whole chapter in my upcoming book, on why it’s really important, if you can do it. It includes tips on what to ask, and how, and the ways you can spot an extra good therapist or one you should. . .pass on. I’ll start referencing the book up there under my name, where it starts “Personal Coaching.” It could be 2–3 months before it’s published and available.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the experience of discussing your relationship with your therapist during therapy? Is this a common practice or should I consider finding a different therapist?
Answer: Yes, it’s a common, and often an important part of therapy. Even if it weren’t, I can’t imagine why you would want to find a different therapist unless the discussion led to that conclusion.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What are some signs that a therapist has ended their sessions with a client?
Answer: No, it should never be about “signs.” Ever. Clients should never be expected to be mind-readers. You decide when your therapy ends, not the therapist (except in very unusual circumstances.) Sadly, some poorly trained or particularly arrogant therapists (there are very few of those, thank heavens), think all those decisions are made by the boss/therapist. If you’re picking up “signs” that the thearpist wants to stop working with you, mention it right away and have a sincere and open discussion of what (if anything) is going on. Maybe the therapist does think you’re coming to an ending point, in their opinion. Part of their job is to provide suggestions and opinions on such things, openly, not with hints and clues. But the final decision is yours, under normal circumstance, though of course it makes sense to consider the therapist’s advice, seriously.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What methods do therapists use to work with shy clients?
Answer: We don’t have templates for various types of clients. Above all, we see each person as a precious, unique individual. Like most experienced properly trained therapists, I don’t rely on methods and techniques modalities. I have to rely on me, and on my client, and the relationship we create. Everything flows from that. If a teacher says “Here’s how to handle a shy client,” (or a teenager, or an elderly person, or a client who is too talkative or a client who won’t make eye contact), offering manipulative tricks, please complaint to the school, drop out of the class and find a teacher who respects individuals, one at a time.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Should the therapist always be the one who closes the door when the patient/client enters the room? Is it weird that the client closes it?
Answer: Never thought of that. Depends on how the office is laid out, and who enters first. I know I’m a psychologist, but I don’t analyze everything, and when I’m not working I don’t analyze much at all.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it considered offensive for clients to address therapists by their first name instead of their professional title?
Answer: In a psychological sense, psychotherapy is pretty intimate. in·ti·mate[ˈin(t)əmət] adjective It would feel a little weird to me to have a full-term client calling me Doctor McPhee all the time. (They can if they want to, and sometimes people like the boundary it signifies, and it’s fine with me because it’s part of the therapy). The majority call me David.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it considered ethical for therapists to give diagnoses through email?
Answer: HIPAA is complicated, and I don’t know all the lastest buzz about HIPAA-compliant platforms, etc. And HIPAA is law, not ethics, though it’s unethical to break certain laws. If you’re talking about mentioning diagnoses in an email, it’s one thing, and think I have to ask a lawyer. In practice, I’d never do it even if all was legal and lovely. Diagnosis is a big deal to most people, and whatever it is, they’re going to have questions, maybe enough questions to fill an hour. I can’t imagine sending a client a diagnosis by email, carrier pigeon, or livried messenger on a bicycle. Imagine this in your inbox from Dr. McPhee “Horace, I considered several possibilities for your diagnosis including Clinical Lycanthropy, and Teezie-Weezies of the left Fantod.” I settled on Involutional Melancholia, Not Otherwise Specified. I forgot to mention that since it’s August, I will be on vaction for the next 4 weeks. Your August appointments have been cancelled. Please contact staff for September through November appointments.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists become annoyed or frustrated with their clients' problems, even if they don't show it?
Answer: Here’s the thing. If the client is annoyed or frustrated with their problems, and I’m an actual, geniune client-centered therapist, not a repeating parrot, I’m into those feelings too, that’s part of any good therapist’s skill set. I don’t feel them the way the client does, but long-practiced accurate empathy lets me experience them at some level. At least most of of the time. And of course I’m going to let it show, some, unless there’s good reason not to. Rogers taught us the basic conditions — unconditional positive regard, genuiness, immediacy, concreteness, etc. Of course I can be annoyed, right alongside my client, with their problems. (I am not annoyed with the client — it could happen, but it’s pretty rare.)

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How can one effectively handle a screaming child in a public setting who refuses to listen to their parents?
Answer: I read the answers. The ones requiring the parents to stop everything and carry the child to the car and go home? Up to them, but what a major inconvenience for the parents, and if it’s a repeated ritual, they’re training the kid in how to be in charge. I love the answer where the parent walks away, a safe space, ignoring the child while still unobtrusively observing. The often true saying “What we attend to grows and increases” applies to potted plants, often to romantic partners, and just about all toddlers. In a different way it works in kid therapy. During the session, the child is the royal focus of everything, with constant but non-intrusive attention from me. If the child gets wild and starts tossing toys, and looks to see my upset and increased interest, I will disappoint them. They’ll see my face turned away and my attention focused on something on my desk, depending. I’m disappearing, emotionally, for at least a moment, and I’ll re-appear when the kid settles a bit. And yes, of course frequent unexplained tantruming can be a symptom of several different problems, and if none of the ordinary common sense remedies aren’t helping, it may be time to check in with a developmental pediatrician (one of my favorite specialties) or a child psychologist.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Why does my therapist end almost every session saying “I wish we had more time”? Is it just a way to tell me the time is finishing?
Answer: Probably, a polite way of saying you’re out of time. If they say it once, it could be true, but not if it’s every time. There was a time I thought I needed to be apologetic when calling time. It’s interesting, these days my consultees and coaching clients seem to be even more aware of the time than I am, and say “Oh, we’ve got five minutes left, I forgot, I wanted to ask you for a book recommendation on meditation. . .” Or something similar. And as I always say, speak up to your therapist. It’s not a big thing, but being open about things like this will be good for your relationship.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What should be done if you have a strong attachment to your psychotherapist and they retire from practicing?
Answer: Grieve. It’s what humans do when we experience a loss. Grief is the healing process that helps us give thanks for what was and accept the loss in the way that’s best for us. It’s a healthy part of every human’s life. I like this little article from the famous Cleveland clinic.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists have clients that they dislike? If so, what are some reasons that may cause a therapist to dislike a client?
Answer: Sure, we can have those feelings for a client. Bossy, insulting, superior, sexist, racist ultra-right wing conspiracy-theorist Ethel? I couldn’t stand her at first. I was polite and generically kind, but she was just as annoying as hell, and I think, no, I’m sure, she was looking for buttons to push and at some level trying to get me to reject her. I had to do some corrective meditations. I started by imagining I was Ethel. What would that be like? Didn’t take long to notice I was feeling scared and lonely when I imagined being in her head. OK, that made me want to help. How do you help a scared and lonely person? Carefully and gently, create an atmosphere of unconditional acceptance and caring, really “getting” her anger and validating it, and her right to express it. Creating a safe and respectful place so she can talk about how she was hurt long ago, or whatever the anger is protecting her from. It went from a helpless “I can’t stand this person, she pisses me off, and makes me want to find an excuse to dump her” to “Ethel is so wounded and lonely and I can be useful, helpful to her.” The things I was reacting to, the things that made me dislike her, were precisely the things that provided little windows and doorways to here heart, to where the pain and loneliness lived. There were times when Ethel still pissed me off — she continued to do her best to annoy and try to trigger rejection — but the agapeic love she inspired and so desperately needed prevailed. Eventually Ethel channeled her feelings and got involved in local politics, and kidded her about becoming a horrible “liberal.” By then her true heart was fully operational and set loose, and she reduced session frequency from twice a week to once a month.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it considered unethical for therapists to date their former clients after the therapy has ended and the client has moved on?
Answer: Yes. Unethical. After a good therapy, the therapist takes up residence in the client’s head, in a way. That’s a good thing. If I’ve worked with my therapist for several months, I’m almost certain to be able to guess what she’d say if I asked her a question about what was going on now, even though we are no longer meeting. I still have conversations with wise old Shalom, who helped me decide about career choices, and also to accept who I was and how I was made. He’d be more than 100 years old now. What if we’d started to hang out as pals after the therapy ended? I can’t imagine it. It would be confusing and almost certainly disappointing, and limit how useful to me he still is. (Not really “he,” but my construction and memory of him as a wise helper and healer and occasional challenger.) What if I’d invited Shalom to go to a baseball game and have some beers after? And we became baseball buddies and companions? It would have been fun at first, maybe, but plain-spoken Shalom would have said, if I invited him to a game “David, David, you know that would spoil the therapy!”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How do psychologists typically react when their clients cry or discuss difficult emotions during therapy sessions?
Answer: It’s not a reaction. Reactions are instantaneous, and involve strong feelings, and having a reaction to a client is rare, though we might find what they say or do a little surprising or unexpected. No, it’s a response. Responses come from our habitual, steady, focused place. I’m listening with my heart, committed to the client and open to hear anything without conditions and am in a state of open positive regard for the person, the way I listen to a performance of a new work at the symphony. I don’t pick it apart in my head, like a critical analyst — I let go and show up as attentive as I can be, letting the new music sweep over me until it’s almost part of me, avoiding any initial judgments. Later, I’ll respond to that deep experience. Let’s say a client has told me a disturbing story of early abuse. I’m there, experiencing with them, as much as I can. When the time is right, I’ll formulate an authentic and heartfelt response that summarize what I’ve heard, and draws attention to the client’s feelings — honoring and validating and bearing authentic witness to them. The reactions that I have (a little spot of anger against the abuser in the story, a bit of shock at how awful that one beating must have been) —those are background noise and if I get into my reactions prematurely, my total attention may be compromised. It’s what’s happening with the client, not what’s happening with me. I can step back and reflect, and process and have an understanding the client may not yet have. That’s my response, and if the time is right and the client is ready, I’ll do my best to put by response into words. I might even share how I reacted to something in the story, if it seems it might be useful, but the response is where the witnessing and holding and healing are.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it typical for therapists to make themselves known as an important figure in their clients' lives, or is their focus solely on helping their clients feel better about themselves?
Answer: The opposite. In many cases we’re actually secret. Even when we aren’t, we don’t “make ourselves known.” And clients might want to “feel better about themselves” but that’s not typical reason for psychotherapy is, though it certainly could be.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists analyse family members, wife, children, and friends most of the time?
Answer: Lord, no! Maybe some kid taking their first abnormal psychology class will spend the first couple of weeks diagnosing various relatives, friends, and movie stars. Most will get bored pretty soon. The deep attention and committed focus that therapy requires — it’s a great job, but that level of concentration requires hard work, and can be tiring. If I’m a house painter I put my brushes and tools away when I’m not working. I’m not going to run around all the time giving everybody’s place a new color, or a touchup. I might love being a therapist (or a painter) but I also have a rich full life where I’m not plying my trade.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How can someone with avoidant attachment disorder be helped if they refuse treatment? Is it possible for them to have healthy and lasting relationships?
Answer: First question: I don’t know how to help someone who doesn’t show up. Second question: Yes, it is very possible for them, through the right psychotherapy (possibly both intensive group work and individual sessions). The avoidant variety of attachment problems can be successfully treated by a combination approach carefully tailored to with the input of the client.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it ethical for a therapist to treat a client if they do not believe their story, but still continue with the treatment?
Answer: If the client believes their own story, and if it’s not hurting anybody, that story is going to carry some truth, some meaning for the client. Accurate empathy and unconditional positive regard guide us to help in any way we can, and it doesn’t depend on the historical accuracy of whatever the client is tellings us. We are not fact-checking for their biography — we are therapists and work with the whole person, including the person who’s “story” isn’t factual.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What will you do as a counselor if you found out that your client wanted to kill a certain person? Will you report it to the police?
Answer: “Wanted” to? That could mean all kinds of things. It could be an exaggerated statement of frustration with some famous politician or molester of little children. “I just want to kill that guy.” I’d follow up, curious about why and how, etc. If the client says, “No, no, I can hardly swat a mosquito, you know that, but he hurt so many people it upsets me.” But— If I have reason to believe that my client may actually have intention, or worse, intention and plan, I could have a “duty to warn” the putative victim, and I’d consult about it, and develop an action plan, quickly if needed. Fact is, I’ve never been in a situation like that, and don’t know anybody personally who has, though I’m sure it’s happened somewhere. Meantime, here’s some information about “Duty to Warn.”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it appropriate to express romantic feelings towards a therapist? How can a client express positive feelings towards their therapist without affecting the therapeutic relationship?
Answer: Entirely appropriate, and a good idea. An inexperienced or poorly trained therapist might freak out and give the client some half-baked shaming speech on boundaries, as if the client having a normal and fairly frequent romantic transference arise in therapy was awful and wrong. Fact is, dealing with the transference in a caring, respectful and skillful way, can be a positive and healthy experience. It’s express the feelings, explore them and resolve them with the help of the therapist.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How should a therapist handle a situation where their client discovers they are also seeing a therapist for their own mental health? Are there any confidentiality concerns in this scenario?
Answer: How would a client “discover” their therapist has a therapist? Yes, that’s the “confidentiality” concern. That’s highly private, protected information, and would take either an unethical disclosure by some professional person or a random chance encounter, or something else. Hard to know. It’s no big deal — we therapists believe in therapy and go a lot — maybe the therapist told the client.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the most unusual thing a client has shared during a therapy session?
Answer: A gerbil named Jezebel, who appeared from a kid’s pocket. Sharing the fact that he wanted to do nude therapy, or at least take off his shirt, shoes, and socks. I said no, but now that I’m old I might just shrug and say “whatever.” Or maybe let him unbutton his shirt or something. I don’t know. I’d have to have somebody make that request and trust my intuition. Still, I’m mostly on screen vs. in person. Nobody ever mentioned this in my training. I’ve mentioned the violinist who brought his instrument to our final session and played so beautifully. Sweet memory. Vivaldi. What else? I’ve had people bring lovely gifts, mostly folks from distant cultures where they assumed it was expected or something. One guy brought two bottles of very expensive Clos du Caillou Chateau neuf de Pape. I couldn’t accept them, but we created a vision of him throwing a party to heal some relationships, and that party became a kind of touchstone we returned to often in the therapy. (I said he could bring a box of Fanny Farmers for the support staff, once a month tops. That worked for him, honored his culture, and the staff liked it. And him. One person thought my office was cold, so she knitted an afghan and gave it as a gift to my office. I had a white leather sofa, and that afghan lived on it for years after (and yes it got regular cleanings.) I could go on, but another time.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it necessary for therapists to know what we discuss with our friends?
Answer: Maybe, if you think it could be important. The therapist creates the safe and healthy boundaries for you, but you’re pretty much in charge of what you want to talk about and why. As your therapist I want to be a committed, interested witness, honoring what you say and how you say it, but I can toss in tips and a little bit of coaching to help you focus and make it clear, and respectfully validate you and what you are sharing. Ultimately you’re the boss of the conversation and where and how it goes. If I say, just as a casual opener, “So how are things at work?” a frequent topic you lead with. If you say “Today I want to talk about my cousin in Peoria! She said some things I want to tell you and get your reaction,” we’re going to Peoria, never mind.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: My new psychiatrist says I don't have BPD. I have C-PTSD, depression & anxiety. What can I do outside of therapy & meds to help myself?
Answer: There are therapies, quite a few of them, to treat c-PTSD, depression and anxiety. I think you mean to ask what’s available outside of “tradtional conversational psychotherapies.” One of the most well known is EMDR, but we could fill a page with various approachs that don’t rely on conversations alone, or even primarily. Take a look:

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How do therapists handle clients sharing their social media activity with them?
Answer: There’s sometimes room for “show and tell” if both therapist and client agree about what and why. I had clients bring their painting, their pottery, their poems, or a printout from social media, etc. to show and maybe discuss. Each therapy is unique. I once had a client, an amazing violinist, bring a violin and play it for me, so beautifully (and so loud) and the support staff gathered in the hall to hear it. It was an important and memorable moment in the therapy.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: When someone says "my doctor", are they referring to their psychiatrist or therapist?
Answer: Where I’m from it means your primary care physician, not a specialist, and most therapists don’t have doctorates, as psychologists do. In the US there are about 80,000 doctoral level psychologists, and they don’t all do psychotherapy by any means, and there are over 200,000 therapists, or more. I have a couple of doctorates, from an education addiction I never got over, and some people in certain situations call me Dr. McPhee, but I’m not “a doctor,” and when the flight attendant says “is there a doctor on board,” I don’t raise my hand (unless someone is having a panic attack — I’m really good with those).

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it common for therapists to share their honest thoughts with their patients during therapy sessions? What are the reasons for this practice?
Answer: Healthy grown humans don’t need reasons to be honest, and being honest isn’t a “practice,” like nose picking or playing the baritone ukelele. Honesty is the norm amoung decent adults who function ethically in a society, even though we fail sometimes. It’s absolutely the norm in psychotherapy. Honesty doesn’t mean telling every fact in your head every moment, which would be boring and annoying and upsetting. Like telling your patient who just got a prescription for the antidepressant Levitratox that 4.73% of patients on it develop itchy patoots within a week. No, honesty isn’t so much about accurate factoids, but about consistent authenticity in a relationship specially psychotherapy. Of course we’re honest and straightfoward with our clients — that’s an essential feature of what we claim therapy is: unconditional positive regard (respect included), genuineness, concreteness, and accurate empathy. For starters.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the protocol for a patient who wants to discontinue psychotherapy? Can a therapist override a patient's decision to stop treatment?
Answer: Only in the most unusual circumstances, such a court-ordered therapy and a few other unusual situations.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the experience like when a therapist suddenly ends therapy without explanation or warning?
Answer: No, that doesn’t happen unless the therapist drops dead or is sent to jail or something. The technical term is “abandonment.” We can get in big trouble for dumping a client without warning or explanation or doing what we can to offer to preserve continuity of care with a new professional, per perhaps in a new setting. Abandonment is a licensing board level offense. Now clients may feel abandoned when the therapist has to end the therapy for good reason (and there are many good reasons ranging from stalking and threats to administrative issues like rarely appearing and failure to pay to the therapist moving to New South Wales or switching careers to interior design). But it’s not abandonment if it’s handled professionally and and in the client’s best interests, and alternative care is offered (even if the client doesn’t accept it.)

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it possible for a person to end their psychotherapy sessions on their own? What is the most respectful way to do so without causing harm to the psychologist/therapist?
Answer: Being fired by a client isn’t harmful. It’s happened to me a few times. There is one time a client fired me and I said “thank god!” No, not to them, but to myself after they left the room. I was really doing my best, and everything I did or said made her angry— cussing fit angry— I’ve never figured out why. I was young then. Now I’d handle it better. Maybe. It’s the only time I think I’ve every said “thank god!” in a clinical setting, out loud

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How should one respond to an unprofessional and dismissive psychologist or therapist?
Answer: C’mon, that’s easy. Walk on by, and if you’re in a situation where you can ask to be transferred to someone else, complain to the boss and ask for that help. It will alert the management about the therapist and they can probably suggest a different person or place.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: I feel like running away from the abuse with my kids. How?
Answer: The hard part is the part that gets you from “I feel like” to “I’ve decided to.” There’s plenty of “how” out there — support for abused parents with kids — governmental and private, including safe place to stay and lots more. When you get to “I’ve decided to get away from the abuse with my kids. How?” Ask it that way, and if you feel OK with saying what state you are in, add that, but only if you’re comfortable. I expect you’ll get some helpful answers.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How should you communicate to your therapist that you want to end therapy? What is the appropriate response from a therapist in this situation?
Answer: “Jack, I’ve decided to end therapy after couple more weeks. I’d like to spend some time talking about it with you, and the best way to conclude our work.” Let Jack know what you’ve decided, and want his help on the best way to for you to do it. Or something like that. Or maybe you’re not absolutely sure, and you want to talk reasons and options and planning.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists become frustrated by constantly giving the same advice?
Answer: I hope so! I hope they are frustrated enough to go work somewhere advice is welcome, like a garden store, or get some extensive in-depth retraining in the basics of their job. Any reasonably common sense adult will be glad to give you advice, or you can get tons of good advice free by writing to Quora or a dozen other similar places. I might give a client suggestions on dog breeds or wine pairings, if it deepened our relationship and their comfort. Any therapist who “constantly gives the same advice” wouldn’t last three days at any place I’ve every studied or worked. Well, maybe three days, but definitely not a whole week. They’d have to have a very weird personality and zero effectiveness or ability to retain clients, and it’s pretty likely they were traumatized in early and middle childhood by ultrarigid hyper-controlling parents who followed them everywhere barking orders about what to do next. Or something like that

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How do therapists determine what to say to help their clients? Is there a specific method or approach they use?
Answer: The specific method is intuition/attention-based spontaneity, as with any open conversation where there’s trust and commitment and the famous unconditional positive regard. In any relationship at that level of trust, plotting certain phrases or targeted sentences to deploy, in advance of a meeting is as foreign and wrong as that type of planning before a regular meeting with a close friend at your normal weekly coffee time together. Your friend would say “what the hell is going on? This is weird. Sounds like you’re giving me a canned speech or something. Geez, just be yourself.”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How would you respond to a mind reader?
Answer: No such thing. I’m watching The Mentalist in the background, and even the Mentalist (played by Simon Baker) freely admits there’s no such thing. Some people, though, are really good at understanding others, people like experienced therapists. We’re trained to pay very close attention and notice the whole person, including all the non-verbal cues, and remembering what the client has said and shown at various times. Typically we don’t show off or get ahead of things by telling the client what they’re going to say next. Or what they’re really worrying about. It’s theirs to share, in their own way, when they want to, when they’re ready. There’s no magic, or at least nothing more magic than steady, caring, deep attention, with a certain kind helper’s unconditional love, and lots of experience. We’re not mind-readers. If we said everything we knew or figured out it would be counter-productive or even rude. It’s the client’s work, not ours, and we provide that famous unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy, in a safe and steady place, so they can do the work. As yes, no matter how smart we think we are as senior therapist, we can be dead wrong, miss the mark, and be totally clueless. Sometimes. That’s another reason we tend to keep our insights to ourselves.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the average cost of a counseling session with a licensed therapist, psychologist, or counselor (excluding psychiatrists)?
Answer: Here’s the difference in pay between therapists and psychologists: most of the figures are in yearly vs. hourly pay, but fairly revealing. Psychologist vs. Therapist Salary Outlook | PsyDPrograms 2022

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is there a psychiatrist or psychologist who can help me for free?
Answer: Lod Kar, roll up you sleeves. I can’t help you because I don’t know were you are, but you can help yourself in about four minutes. Go online and type in name name of your state followed by “free psychotherapy.” Like I did: “Minnesota free psychotherapy.” There were pages and pages of all kinds of free care, private and pubic. I figure you’ll get the same in your state (or province), expect in California the list will be really long and in South Dakota, shorter, but every state will have what you need, maybe there’s a hoop or two, or you’ll have to make some calls, and maybe you’ll have to start with a therpist vs. a psychologist, but the help is there.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What makes a person technically a client of a therapist? I am participating in reunification therapy with my child. I pay half. Am I also a client since it is reunification therapy that is court ordered in our mediation agreement?
Answer: You’re already involved with Family Court or the equivalent, and there are lots of legal papers etc. Assuming your reunification therapist is ethical and well trained (and most family forensic practitioners are), you have signed a service agreement that (should) spell out all the relationships and roles and limits, and on and on. The “am I a client” is almost certainly in there, along with a lot of other items.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What training is required for counselors/therapists to become licensed?
Answer: Normally the right master’s degree and a few thousand hours of supervised experience, and passing a challenging test. It varies from state to state. Psychologists need a doctorate, but the rest is similar.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: When I wrote messages to my therapist by email expressing how positive I feel about them, they always skipped that part to adress the other things in the email leaving me embarrassed. Why are they doing that?
Answer: First, a big statement about therapy. It doesn’t work well asynchronously. (Is that a word?) I mean it doesn’t work very well to send written notes back and forth. I’d skip the positive feelings part too, that needs to dealt with in person. It’s a core part of the therapy. You can write sweet affirmations to your girlfriend or you mom and dad. We get no training in therapy-by-letter, and it’s a lame way to do psychotherapy — like reading the script of a movie vs. seeing a movie. All the best stuff, or the vast majority of it, is non verbal, either situaton. Not so much what you say but how you say it. If you’re having trouble speaking during sessions, go ahead and write the messages, but don’t send them, bring them to the session, where the important stuff happens — read them out loud and let the thearpist respond and interact with you, real time.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How do you know if you’re just doing or saying something in therapy to garner attention from your therapist?
Answer: I’ve been a licensed psychologist since the time Nixon resigned amid Watergate and Ford took over, seen thousands of clients and been a client myself. Never, mind I still can’t answer that question, and worrying about it will just be a distraction. If you are worried anyway, tell the therapist and they’ll help you sort it out. The last thing we therapists want you to do is to monitor yourself and try to figure out all the various intentions and motivations underlying what you say. Your therapy is one of the safest places you can be with a trained, caring, committed human, who wants you to say and express anything that pops into your head, without worrying about it. Yeah, I know there a few lemons out there, but most therapists want to engage with you, unconditionally, with no agenda but your welfare. If you wan’t more “attention” from your therapist, you can just say so, and together you can figure out the what and the how of it, or let it go and speak from the depths of your heart. This is your precious time, unlike any other time. You can do anything you want with it, but this old man says if you’re monitoring, editing, or otherwise limiting yourself, you might be missing something wonderful. But it’s always up to you.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it advisable to take a break from therapy when experiencing medical issues that affect emotional processing and reflection, with permission from the therapist?
Answer: You don’t need permission from your therapist any more that you need permission from your personal trainer, if your medical issues will complicate or interfere with your therapy in a way that makes you decide to pause your therapy. That said, therapy can be modified to suit your situation, and might be useful with a temporarily modified approach and frequency — entirely up to you, of course.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists become angry with their clients if they refuse to discuss certain topics, such as childhood trauma?
Answer: I guess they could, being human, mess up and act like an angry policeperson interrogating you, which would be a bad kind of unethical, and depending on how bad it was, actionable if you made a complaint. Such a therapist, no doubt, has a lot of problems, and could probably use some help. Licensing boards may require the licensee to take courses, go to supervision, or get other help, which is usually a good thing for the therapist and their future clients.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How does one become an APA-certified clinical psychologist?
Answer: That would be a long wait. The American Psychological Association accredits (certifies) training programs, not individual psychologists. There is an organizaton, the American Board of Professional Psychology, which does certify, in their way. You have be licensed, etc., complete a lot of preliminaries, then pass an oral exam administered by a team of psychologists. I was certified in counseling psychology, and could use ABPP after my name, and bypass some minor governmental barriers to something. I think it helped me get a job one time. My memory tells me that they certify in clinical, counseling, forensics, maybe more. For more reliable information, go here:

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it common for therapists to feel offended or take it personally if their patients do not remember what was discussed in previous sessions?
Answer: Not at all. There are tons of reasons for not remembering something, especially if the memory is difficult or traumatic. As a therapist I’d notice the forgetting, put a mental pin it, and move on with whatever the client wanted to talk about. No need to intepret it or make something of it when it happens.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the proper title for a clinical psychologist?
Answer: The standard degree for a clinical psychologist is a doctorate, so you’re pretty safe with “Doctor” followed by the last name. If they have a higher title, it’s customary to use the highest one. Like “Professor,” or a whole range of religious titles, like Rabbi, and Father, and Bishop, and Pastor, and Sister (for a nun), etc. People in any of those jobs could be clinical psychologists. Also politicians. You use their elected office, like Senator, etc. or Sheriff, etc. The list goes on. All those people could be clinical psychologists, but you call them the higher name, rank, or office.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Could multiple personality disorder make a male feel that he is a female if one of the multiple personalities in multiple personality disorders is female?
Answer: We actually call it “Dissociative Identity Disorder,” which is a pretty good description. Here’s a little reading on it. Dissociative Identity Disorder (Multiple Personality Disorder)

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the purpose of therapists having their own therapist? Can therapists also be clients of their own colleagues?
Answer: I’d say any therapist is a “colleague,” whoever and where ever, since we do the same job. We don’t hire our friends or associates as therapists. In our business we’re pretty clear how important boundaries are in making therapy work.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists typically have their own therapists or do they rely on friends and family for support?
Answer: I don’t have statistics, but I’m pretty sure we therapists go to therapy a lot more then folks in general. We know how useful it is, even when we don’t have any major problems. I’ve gone for a few sessions every time I had a major job or life change, just to it through. Always glad I did

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Why do some mental health agencies hire snobby people as therapists?
Answer: Snobby people? Here’s what I found out about snobby, so I can think about all the people I’ve hire, to see if I can remember who was snobby. Snobby is an adjective used to describe someone who is condescending, patronizing, or socially exclusive 1. It is also used to describe someone who has an offensive air of superiority and tends to ignore or disdain anyone regarded as inferior 2. The word is informal and disapproving 3. It is used to describe a person who respects and likes only people who are of a high social class, or a person who has extremely high standards and is not satisfied by the things that ordinary people like. I do remember a very young, newly-minted psychiatrist, sitting in a coffee shop near the clinic. We were considering taking her on, in spite of her lack of post-residency experience. She told me how she would always refer people out (only for CBT) — like the psychiatrist tells the psychotherapist what specific methods to apply. That would be like me sending all clients to a psychiatrist for Abilify, because I know best. I let it slide. Then she said she’d been hoping to work at a clinic where the providers were “Ph.D. and up.” Since there’s no higher degree than Ph.D., and only a few medical doctors get one, I decided at that point she lacked interpersonal skills that would be need in busy multidisciplinary clinic with a strong collaborative atmosphere. She intoduced herself as “Doctor” so-and-so, and clearly expected to be addressed that way. She called me David (in spite of my two doctorates, and being 25 years older than she was). Everybody calls me David, but from her it sounded like I was being put in my place. I’m sure she grew up and became a kind, caring practitioner who could relate with empathy and respect to patients and colleagues, even the ones who weren’t “Ph.D. and up,” and all the superior snobiosity melted away. I just didn’t want her to practice on us.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it possible for a therapist to refer a patient to another therapist for the sake of their mental health and well-being?
Answer: The referent for “their” isn’t clear. You’ve got three possibles: therapist number one, the patient, and therapist number two. Or maybe you mean all three, suggested by the plural “their.” Whichever it is, there’s some need or motivation to transfer a client to somebody else, and the question asks “is it possible?” I’d say it’s possible that a therapist would refer a patient out for somebody’s health and well-being, or everybody’s, definitely possible. They and their have taken a horrible beating, totally apart from gender neutrality and pronoun referents

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Psychotherapy only works when the client fully commits to their growth and their contribution to the process. Do you agree with this?
Answer: No. That’s kind of an ideal, perfect therapy. Nobody’s perfect. A partial commitment is a commitment, good enough for me. A bad week when the client’s contribution isn’t much, is still good enough just because they showed up. You’ve been to weddings, and listened to the vows and the preacher’s loftly predictions about perfect love, and you know even a great marriage has ups and downs because they’re both humans. Same with therapy. There’s a commitment, and that means showing up and doing your best and that’s absolutely enough. “Fully commits?” I have had clients who obsess about being perfect clients. Normally, we have to get past that phase before they can relax and be their beautiful plain old selves. No, psychotherapy usually works when both therapist and client show up.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do counsellors/therapists disclose the books they are reading as part of their training/education to their clients? How does this disclosure impact the clients and/or the therapist?
Answer: I sometimes recommend a book. For example, Your True Home by the Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh. A very, very gentle introduction to meditation. (I don’t always call it “meditation” — some folks are put off by the word.) Hanh has a little half-page thought or idea for every day. A two or three minute read, tops, but something you can take with you for the whole day. I recommend it to students and consultees too — we need to be in a sort of open-hearted, open-minded place when we’re doing psychotherapy.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: If a client is a published author, would a therapist consider or be allowed to buy the client’s book online (not directly from the client)?
Answer: I’ve got a book coming out. It’s a practical manual for getting the most out of therapy. All proceeds go the children’s grass roots charities. Get the Most From Therapy: McPhee’s Essential Manual. It’s supposed to be available everywhere in about in 2–3 months, I hope. My clients and supervisees would absolutely be allowed to buy it. I’d encourage them to order a copy — but I definitely wouldn’t sell it from my office.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the significance of a psychologist or psychiatrist saying "I need to see you more"?
Answer: The professional is not a well-qualified speaker of English, at any level of nuance. Be a little careful about a person whose language skills are marginal. If I were watching a role play where the doctor said that, I’d honk my little horn and say “No. You don’t use “I need” with a client, and you’d never follow it with “to see you more!” No matter the speaker’s intention, it sounds like the client is supposed to be taking care of the therapist’s needs, rather than the strictly required vice-versa attitude. A vulnerable client could easily hear it as declaration of love and desire. No. A skilled English speaker would say “I wonder if we could talk about the frequency of our sessions.” Or something like that. If the client says yes, the doctor might say “I was thinking about possibly meeting a little more often, if you like, for a few sessions, to talk about your mom’s death, or. . .continue as we are. . ? Any statement from a therapist to a client that starts with “I need you. . .” or worse, “I need to see you more. . .” no matter the intention. . . could be a bit of a problem.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can I request a specific therapist or gender?
Answer: You can request any gender or race or ethnicity or age (go for the old ones), or religion or gender identity or sexual orientation or hair color or political party or favorite baseball team. It’s one of the few areas where you get to “discriminate,” the way you would with dating. Of course, the clinic can offer you only the people they have available. No clinic or hospital or agency, private or public, is obliged to find you someone who meets your preferences or prejudices, etc, but most places will honor your request if they reasonably can.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists typically have mirrors in their therapy rooms? What is the purpose of having a mirror in a therapy room?
Answer: I always kept a hand mirror in my desk drawer, for clients who’d been crying a lot or something, clients who wanted to fix their faces before they left the room. Tissue, of course, wipes, that kind of thing. They weren’t often used, but it was nice to have them if needed. I also had some drugstore reading glasses for people who were signing documents and forget their own. I even had a big empty coffee can with a cover in case somebody, usually a kid, had to upchuck. I needed the coffee can no more than a couple of times a year, but I was glad to have it when I did.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists ever realise that two of their patients know each other and talk about each other in therapy, when they themselves don't know they share a therapist? What are the ethical concerns in this scenario?
Answer: It can happen if you see kids, say if you routinely see kids and teens, and there are big public or private schools in your area. It could happen a lot if you have a reputation as a good kid therapist. I’ve been in that situation a few times, and it quickly becomes an ingrained habit to compartmentalize the brain. One kid comes in and talks about this football player she likes and I realize I saw the football player last year, for what I have no idea. I’m watching a TV series softly in the background as I type this. I know the actors and a bit about their histories, from appearances on talk shows, but I’m only seeing the characters they are playing. It’s the story. Same with therapy. I’m into the person in front of me at the time, and their story, who knows them somewhere else.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What type of therapist has confidentiality rules about discussing sessions outside of the therapy room?
Answer: I know you don’t mean massage therapists and physical therapists, though they have ethical codes too. I figure you mean psychotherapists, and if you do, the answer would be “all types.”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How can someone find the right therapist or psychiatrist after having negative experiences with them in the past? Is it possible to know if a therapist or psychiatrist is not a good fit before trying them out?
Answer: Excellent question. I devote a whole chapter to it in my upcoming book Get the Most from Psychotherapy: McPhee’s Essential Handbook. In the book I suggest interviewing a possible therapist, with sample questions and approaches, and what to look for.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What would happen if I admitted my sadistic desires to my therapist?
Answer: You’d get a response from a safe person in safe and private space, a response that could be useful to you in understanding and caring for yourself.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it considered inappropriate to have a preference for your therapist?
Answer: No, picking a therapist (if you have a choice) is really important. It’s going to be a working, hopefully healing relationship. Nothing wrong with being clear on the type of person you want as your therapist.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is there hope/a therapist for me? My therapist (trauma specialist) abandoned me abruptly due to reenactment and acting out and said I destroy the therapist. She has made me believe it is all my fault, that I am wrong and not good enough for therapy.
Answer: I’d have to know exactly what reenactment and acting out means, to answer the question. If a qualified trauma therapist ended therapy with you, they must have thought it was a big deal. In order t help, I’d need to know more, if I were the person arranging a referral for you. Some therapists would probably be fine, especially if they have talent and experience. In these situations I want to have a fairly clear image of the client in my head and then imagine them working with various therapists I know. It’s the way, when you’re hiring somebody for a job, you’re likely to imaging that person doing that job, to see how it feels and fits.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What are the distinctions between a marriage and family therapist and a clinical psychologist?
Answer: Maybe not much. As a psychologist, I’ve done lots of marriage and family work. Marriage and family counselors certainly use psychological approaches of various kinds. A common license is LMFT (licensed marriage and family therapist), with requres the equivalent of a master’s degree. Psychologists normally have doctorates. That doesn’t mean we’re better therapists, just that we have a broader scope that includes testing and evaluation, etc., in addition to psychotherapy.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What would a therapist think if a client shows up wearing baggy, layered clothes in the summer?
Answer: There’s potential medical stuff I’m not qualified to discuss, but it could mean several different, other things. I’d probably say “I notice you’re wearing lots of extra clothing and it make me curious about what’s going on for you.” That could prompt a shrug, or some talk about it, or maybe talk later. I’ll learn what’s up soon or later, when the client is ready. They control the timing, and I’m not going to grab control by asking a lot of questions.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it concerning for a therapist if their patient refuses to discuss certain topics, such as abuse or trauma, during therapy sessions?
Answer: It’s timing. And the client is in charge of timing. It’s not that the client “refuses to discuss. . .” It’s that they “hasn’t yet begun to explore. . .”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do therapists ever feel used by their clients during or after therapy sessions? If so, how do they cope with this feeling?
Answer: “Used by clients?” I hope so. The basic precept of my life, the one that sustains and motivate me as an old person, is this: “Be useful to others.” That’s my secret, the one I reveal when people ask why I’m happy. (I can provide philosophical, scriptural, and poetic reasons for the precept, but no need. Its self-proving.) A client says I’ve been really useful? I thanks gods it’s so, and thank the client for the wonderful validation. Response to the feeling of usefulness? Joy, and thanks to whatever higher power made all this.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How should a counselor deal with the limitations of existential therapy?
Answer: As a philosophy major, I’m skeptical of approaches focused on . . . a philosophy. Our personalities attract our philosophies. It has always been so. If I’m full of anxiety, understanding the meaning of life, or being required to, could make me even more nervous. The best way to “deal with it” is to deploy the approach only when clearly suited to and desired by the client. It could be a good ice-breaker until you get to the real issues.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the appropriate attire for a first therapy session, both as a client and as a therapist?
Answer: In late autumn in Minnesota, for a male therapist, good quality jeans with a conservative cut, a fine T-shirt or light sweater, and a tweedy sport coast, all in earth tones except the jeans. Just kidding. Anything that provides a non-distracting level of simplicity and modesty is “appropriate.”

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it possible for someone without empathy to work as a therapist or counselor for children?
Answer: If you understand “empathy” to be a funny inside tickle of special warmth and caring. Yes. If you understand empathy to be a conscious, lasting decision to act in a consistently loving way, aware and understanding of the thoughts and feeling of children in their care, also yes, sweet tickle or not.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: I attend a church where the congregation is down to 5 members with a pastor who is the only leadership position of the church still attending. Can he quit and lock the church up legally?
Answer: Depends whose name is on the deed or lease. He can probably quit unless he’s got a contract, but closing the buiding? Probably not. This is a totally amateur opinion from a former pastor, not an attorney.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How do you explore the emotional side of a topic in therapy, beyond the facts? For example if a client felt upset about not being able to book a session one week but understands it was due to conflicting schedules - what else do you talk about?
Answer: We used to used the phrase “getting in touch with your feelings.” If there were an upset about an appointment, I’d invite the client to express it fully, and explore it. Maybe it connects with feelings of being overlooked, ignored, or unimportant in the past. Now we have some actual hurt and anger about an appointment not given, and we can explore the old feelings underneath that, and bear witness and honor and validate those old feelings.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists become emotionally attached to their patients/clients? How do they handle this and how common is it?
Answer: I don’t see little kids these days, and yes, I miss them. I used to see a lot of kids ages 4 on up. Sometimes I’d worry about them — not obsessively, but they’d pop into my head and I think about the abuse and little feelings of anger and protectiveness would come up for a moment or two. I thought that was a good sign. I genuinely cared about them, but also kept enough objectivity so I could be useful during sessions. If I never, ever thought about them at all I think I’d be worried enough to bring it up to my supervisor/consultant.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can someone become addicted to therapy or psychotherapy? Is it possible to have too many therapists?
Answer: Addicted? Too strong a word, but people get dependent on therapy. Maybe a bad thing, but maybe not. Folks who are seriously and persistently mentally ill can survive and even thrive with frequent high quality therapy, often augmented by the right medication and support. I call that a healthy dependency, the way I depend on certain medications to keep me healthy in these years when I am seriously and persistently . . .old. Too many therapists is probably worse than having too many medical doctors. The doctors do tend to keep track of all the meds the patient is on, whatever the source, and the primary docs talk to specialists. Less so with the independent therapists — people normally have only one at a time. We frown on having a handful of therapists, unless they are serving distinct functions. A hypnotherapist helps with the physical pain of rheumatoid arthritis, and there’s a psychologist who’s doing EMDR related to early trauma, and a pastoral counselor focusing on spirituality and medication. That could work just fine, and any number of clients could benefit from having several types of therapists — you could add a Reiki practitioner and a music therapist too. It’s only too many therapists when they are working at cross purposes, or not swimming in their own lanes.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What should a patient with anxiety and depression expect during their first counseling/therapy session if they have never received mental health services before?
Answer: Gentle, cautious, low key but clearly caring unconditional attention. Not a lot of questions or advice. Just connecting in a safe space. Willingness to listen to anything you say, or being OK with silent waiting until you’re ready. Waiting for you to say something, if you want. Or making little easy statements to you, but no demands. If you’re in my office, I might make a few guesses based on what I see, or think I see, and notice how they land. Generally, you should experience the comfort of another human who is fully present to you, without demands or direction, and ready to respond when you’re ready for a response.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Should my new online therapist be typing and taking notes on her computer while I am talking, not looking at me? When I asked, she was angry and said maybe I should find someone else.
Answer: I completely agree with her. You should find a fully human organism, capable of and will to have an authenic connection with another human organism, without cyber-assistance. Being on a screen is bad enough, without the zero eye contact except with her keyboard.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: What is the choice of drug for a cestode?
Answer: Not sure, but I want it fast, based on this portrait of the parasite: I don’t even want to read this article below, but I honor your question by looking up the answer for on the latest interventions. In my youth I was involved part-time with a clinic, and had the experience of watching an endlessly long cestode being expelled (with a few helping tugs by staff) from the, uh, large intestine of a person. Even writing about it 60 years later gives me a major case of the teezie-weezies of the fantod.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: If you are not interested in medication, do you need a psychiatrist?
Answer: Maybe. Psychiatrists have more than drugs to offer. Take a look: 6 alternative therapies for mental health problems

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it appropriate for therapists to give advice to their clients? Can giving advice be beneficial in therapy?
Answer: Yes and yes. Sometimes the advice itself is great. More important, relying on another person and asking their advice can be a healing act of trust, and the very act could be very beneficial. Ultimately, the most important thing is therapy can be the relationship with the therapist, whatever the actual advice is.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do individuals with dissociative identity disorder (DID) typically have a specialized doctor for their condition, or does their therapist/psychiatrist treat all of their personalities?
Answer: Most experienced psychologists and many qualified therapists can work with folks with DID. Some people with DID aren’t looking for treatment for that, but have other issues that concern them. They might routinely bring one alter to therapy. A while back, a person with DID asked me how many folks I had seen in my career with DID. I said “not that many, maybe 10 or12.” He answered with a chuckle “You’ve seen lot more than that, you just didn’t know it because that’s not why they were seeing you, and you only saw the one alter, the therapy alter.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: How can you get comfortable with your therapist (since therapists analyse everything you do and don’t)?
Answer: Fuhgeddaboudit. I fear you’ll be uncomfortable. How could you ever be comfortable if you think that’s what therapists are like. Your attitude toward what you imagine “therapists” to be will make it impossible. You’ve read all our minds, in advance, before even meeting one of us. It’s like asking how to get comfortable in a restaurant, since they all spit in the soup, or talking to liberals since they all want to kill babies. See, in therapy, we treat you with unconditional positive regard, as a unique and precious human being. We open our ears and our hearts as we begin to discover you as a person and what you seek. I’ve been in this business 40 years, seeing therapy clients, teaching students, and loving it, and I would have no idea about how to go about “analyzing everything that people do.” What would be the point of that? We know better than anybody that analysis is paralysis.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can therapists discuss their experiences within therapy with friends and family without violating confidentiality, as long as they do not mention any names?
Answer: Just hiding names isn’t enough. My protecting my clients’ privacy is part of what shapes me as a therapist, even when they won’t know I’m talking about them anonymously. It’s an attitude, a habit, and my family and friends would be shocked if I told them stories about clients, named or unnamed. Example: for teaching purposes I talk about highly fictionalized “clients” here on Quora and in my upcoming book, but they are disguised beyond recognition, even by themselves. Often they are composites. Client stories are not meant to entertain, ever, no matter how well disguised.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Can individuals be involuntarily committed to a psychiatric facility without having committed a crime?
Answer: Those situations are more likely to arise when the patient is a danger to self, rather than to others. It could be both, but most mentally ill people are not violent or a threat. It varies a lot from place to place, but the hospital can keep people for a short period, a day, three days, on the say-so of medical staff. Beyond that, in serious cases, they may get a court-ordered “commitment” for a specified period. Some places they may need an additional court order to medicate with neuroleptics and or ECT (shock therapy). For most patients, there’s no major crime involved.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Is it appropriate to terminate a therapist for not being helpful and not listening to your concerns?
Answer: You can end therapy any time, if you’re an adult and not court-ordered or something. I confess I’m worried about “terminating a therapist,” or having Arnold Schwarzenegger do it for you, but I trust you mean “ending thearpy.” Not ending the therapist, even one who doesn’t even listen. Your question make me think you really do want good thearpy, and there tons of it out here. If you dump the current one (and discuss it with them, you’ll probably learn something from a final closure session.) If you move on, be sure to interview your next therapist before you hire time. There’s a whole chapter in my new book, which should be out soon. (What to ask, and how it ask it for maximum learning).

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Do clients have to pay for their first counselling/therapy session, even if they are unsure if the counsellor is a good fit for them?
Answer: Yes. If it’s an actual psychotherapy session. If it’s a brief interview of the therapist, you asking questions to see if you want to hire them — and you both agree to that, typically no. They don’t want you to talk about your issues until you’re actually a client — instead you’ll ask “do you have experience with xyz?” Or “how would you handle abc,” or there could be a bit of a HIPAA mess.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: I think my therapist might be gay. Can I discontinue service with him for that reason alone?
Answer: Good news (sort of). You can dump your therapist for letting his mustache grow too long or growing one in the first place, or for having a Canadian accent (calling progress ‘pro-gress,’ with a long “o.” Of for being Black or not being black. This is one of those areas, like dating, where you get to discriminate at will. You can require a therapist to be tall and bald and South Asia. Anything. Really, it might be dumb to act on your prejudices, but in therapy, as in dating, you get to do it. If you can’t find one that meetings all your specs who is also on your insurance, of course you are out of luck. Just as you can reject any of us for excessive nose hair or being from the Czech Republic, of course we can reject you too (unless we’re employed by an agency that assigns people to therapists, or maybe we’re students, same deal.) And of course no clinic or agency or hospital is required to provide you with someone who meets all your prejudiced criteria. You want a First Nations therapist? You’ll have to find one who is willing to take you. (In your case, someone you imagine to be guaranteed heterosexual, though I’m not sure how you would do that, or why). Two-way street.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: Am I allowed to not continue therapy with my therapist for any reason, even after one visit, or will he get mad?
Answer: That initial session is often called an “intake,” and it’s understood that either the therapist or the client may decide not to continue into the therapy for a lot of reasons.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
Question: If a therapist has a client disclosed to him threats to others. The therapist is having trouble determine if the threat is real. Can the therapist consult a lawyer and other therapist as second option and not be considered breaching confidentiality?
Answer: Of course you can consult, and the question would be carefully hypothetical. It would also seem a little odd for a thearpist to ask a lawyer to assess your client’s mental state and potential for harm, though the right lawyer could explain the relevant statues and describe how and whether they have been enforced in your jurisdiction.

Name: David McPhee, Ph.D.
